P1.evidence: No frame and no agreement on a follow-up whose whole purpose was to reach a decision. The opening question was warm but open-ended enough to hand control away — 'tell me, like, where are you at right now? How do you feel?' — and the prospect used it to open with his competitor research and then the word 'pricey'. Setter read-back not applicable.

P2.evidence: Baseline belongs to the original closing call, which is not in this batch.

P3.evidence: The best move on the call was refusing to negotiate before re-establishing the why: 'Before we get into the numbers, which are, of course, are playing an important role, what is the main thing that you're actually wanting to ... what's the outcome that you're looking for in this program?' That produced health, the disc and the blood pressure, and the rep followed with 'if health is the main reason that you came here for'. It then stopped. The future-state question was framed around the money rather than the outcome — 'in two years, five years, ten years ... will you be thinking about the 6K that you paid' — and family was gestured at in a subordinate clause and never developed. No reflect-back and no drive to identity.

P4.evidence: Past attempts and root cause belong to the original call.

P5.evidence: The nearest thing to a consequence frame was inverted into a price-justification question — 'down the line, like, in two years, five years, ten years, when you actually look healthy, feel healthy, look better, show up for you, for your family, will you be thinking about the 6K that you paid for this?' That asks about regret over the spend, not about the cost of doing nothing, and the prospect answered it accordingly. The material was sitting there unused: a disc problem, high blood pressure the prospect himself calls lifestyle-driven, and his own line about a slope downwards. None of it was turned into two years of no change.

P6.evidence: No belief question and no isolation at any point, which matters here because the prospect twice signalled that the decision was already made and only the number was open — 'I have everything decided' and 'I know I make my commitment, but I want to do it. Let's find a good price.' That is a yes waiting to be confirmed and converted, and it was never tested, so the call ended with the rep owing a discount rather than the prospect owing a decision.

P11.evidence: No agreement and no payment; nothing was reachable.

objection_plays.detail: Money was the entire call and not one scripted move ran. No isolation, no 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place', no permission question, and none of the six financial-picture questions — which would in fact have been the right diagnostic here, because they would have established quickly that there is no affordability constraint at all and that this is a value and negotiation problem. Instead the rep produced a cheaper tier within four minutes of the word 'pricey' and then agreed to shop a further discount internally.

Discount demand from a buyer who can pay. This is a script gap not currently documented in the playbook alongside the clinical-fit and cheaper-substitute gaps. The prospect is not asking how to afford it, he is asking to be met on price as a matter of commercial principle — 'it has to be fair from my perspective ... these prices, they are not like hammered on the concrete' — and he has explicitly made the purchase conditional on a concession. Objection C assumes incapacity to pay and has nothing for a capable buyer who simply negotiates. The rep, with no play and no authority, invented a tier and then escalated.

Comparable competitor at the same price. 'I can get the same, for the same money, training with the guy, two times per week ... not so far away from my office', plus several online coaches in Denmark with identical transformation positioning. The documented gap in the playbook covers a cheaper alternative that worked; this is a same-priced local alternative the prospect has not tried, which needs proof of differentiation rather than a business-model argument. The rep's only differentiator was his own testimony that he uses the programme himself.

notes: One genuinely good instinct — refusing to talk numbers until the outcome was restated — and then the call was lost to the negotiation. The rep took three price positions in eleven minutes and ended owing the prospect a discount, which hands the next conversation to the buyer. The concrete coaching point is that this prospect said twice that he had already decided; the move was to close on the decision and hold the price, not to produce a cheaper tier the prospect immediately priced as worse value.
